prompt: You run the pipe ping-pong benchmark from the lesson pinned to one core. 100,000 round trips take 0.5 s. Under the alternating hand-off model, what upper estimate does this give for the average scheduler-switch contribution per hand-off?

options.explanation: That is the time per *round trip*. Each round trip contains two switches.
Correct. 0.5 s / 100,000 = 5 µs per round trip, and with 2 switches per round trip that's 2.5 µs each, including the syscall overhead.
This divides by four, treating the four syscalls as four switches. There are four syscalls but only two switches.
This is out by a factor of 10: 0.5 s / 100,000 is 5 µs, not 50 µs.

workedExample:
Turn the total time into a time per round trip, then split it between the two switches each round trip contains:

```formula
t_trip = T / N
t_trip = 500,000,000 ns / 100,000
t_trip = 5,000 ns
t_switch = t_trip / 2
t_switch = 5,000 ns / 2 = 2,500 ns
where
T: the total measured time, 0.5 s = 500,000,000 ns
N: the number of round trips, 100,000
t_trip: the time for one round trip, in nanoseconds (ns)
t_switch: an upper estimate of average scheduler-switch contribution per hand-off, in nanoseconds (ns), assuming at least two hand-off switches per round trip
ns: nanosecond, one billionth of a second; 1,000 ns = 1 µs
s: second
µs: microsecond, one millionth of a second
In words: a 5 µs round trip contains two hand-offs, so the average scheduler-switch contribution per hand-off is no more than the measured 2.5 µs half-trip under this model.
```

It is a model-based upper estimate of the average contribution because those 2.5 µs also cover IPC and syscall work; it does not bound every individual switch. Pinning to one core (`taskset -c 0`) makes sure you measure switches, not cross-core wake-ups.

prompt: You run the ping-pong benchmark without pinning, and the two processes land on different cores. What are you now mostly measuring?

options.text: The same context-switch cost, just less precisely
options.explanation: On separate cores each process can sleep and wake on its own core, so the timing is dominated by something else.

options.text: Cross-core wake-up latency: signalling the other core and waking its sleeping task
options.explanation: Separate-core placement can add remote wake-up communication and idle-state exit work. An IPI is not required on every hop; measure the actual placement and wait behaviour.

options.text: Only the syscall cost, since no switches occur
options.explanation: Switches still happen on each core (to and from idle), but the main cost is the cross-core signalling.
TLB shootdowns happen when shared mappings change. A pipe write doesn't change any mappings.

workedExample: Separate cores add inter-core communication, possible remote wake-ups and idle-state exit costs. A wake-up need not always require a new IPI if the receiving CPU is already running suitable work or polling. Pinning both tasks to one logical CPU removes cross-core placement from the experiment, but the timing still includes IPC, syscalls and other scheduling interference.
